{{Short description|Shrine in Fuchū, Tokyo, Japan}} {{More footnotes|date=April 2010}} {{Expand Japanese|大國魂神社 (府中市)|date=November 2013}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōkunitama Shrine
大國魂神社 | image = Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|2.87|N|139|28|44.19|E|type:landmark|display=inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = [[Ōkuninushi]]
[[:en:Kunitama|Okunitama]] | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. ''Asian folk culture studies'' (8), 1-32. *Nittamachi Yoshinao 1997 The Symbolism of The Expression in Touka. ''Research memoirs of the Kobe Technical College'' 35, 89-94. *Miyazaki Takeshi 1997 A Study of a Traditional Event Utagaki in Tsugaru Area.7 『日本歌謡研究』 37, 73-83. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category}} * [http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ Official website] {{in lang|ja}} {{Shinto shrine}} {{Coord|35|40|02.4|N|139|28|44.4|E|source:jawiki_scale:25000|display=title}} {{Ōtori Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Sōja shrines}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]] [[Category:Fuchū, Tokyo]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] }} [[sn:Ōkunitama Shrine]] [[en:Ōkunitama Shrine]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] {{Commons category|Okunitama-jinja, Fuchu}} [[fa:معبد اوکونیتاما]] [[fr:Ōkunitama-jinja]] [[ja:大國魂神社]] [[zh:大國魂神社]]

{{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q611678]] Wikidata name: Ōkunitama Shrine [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:37, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Shrine in Fuchū, Tokyo, Japan}} {{More footnotes|date=April 2010}} {{Expand Japanese|大國魂神社 (府中市)|date=November 2013}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōkunitama Shrine
大國魂神社 | image = Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{coord|35|40|2.87|N|139|28|44.19|E|type:landmark|display=inline}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = [[Ōkuninushi]]
[[:en:Kunitama|Okunitama]] | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = ''[[nagare-zukuri]]'' | festival = | leadership = }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. 大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|qid=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|qid=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. 大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|qid=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|qid=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|qid=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. [[sn:commons:Category:Okunitama-jinja, Fuchu]][[en:Ōkunitama Shrine]][[fa:معبد اوکونیتاما]][[fr:Ōkunitama-jinja]][[ja:大國魂神社]][[zh:大國魂神社]] {{afc comment|Wikidata entry [[d:Q611678]] Wikidata name: Ōkunitama Shrine [[User:Immanuelle|Immanuelle]] ([[User talk:Immanuelle|talk]]) 10:37, 11 June 2025 (UTC)}} {{Short description|Shrine in Fuchū, Tokyo, Japan}} {{More footnotes|date=April 2010}} {{Expand Japanese|大國魂神社 (府中市)|date=November 2013}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Ōkunitama Shrine
大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|WD=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|WD=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (24), 47-60. *中里 亮平 2008 Festivals and ''Influential'' members of the community: the case of the Kurayami-matsuri Festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu-shi, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (23), 51-64. *Tsuruga Eisuke 2007 Possibility on recovery of the humanity, concerned with festival reciprocity : Through the Fuchu Kurayami Matsuri researches. ''Education for sustainable development'' 6, 105-112. *Mogi Sakae, Shimada Kiyoshi 1989 The Kurayami Matsuri at Okunitama Shrine in Fuchu ''Transactions of the institute for Japanese culture and classics'' 64, 140-207, *杉浦 翔子 2006 A study of the chief priest system of the plum wine drinking ritual held at Owari-no-Okunitama Jinja 『皇学館論叢』 39(6), 36-63, *Koide Goro 1983 On Argonauta argo Housed in the Okunitama Shrine.『ちりぼたん』 14(1), 21. ===Utagaki=== *糸永 正之 2009 ''Utagaki'' in Bhutan: the verification of face-to-face interaction through fixed-verse songs. 大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|WD=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|WD=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. 大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|WD=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|WD=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (24), 47-60. *中里 亮平 2008 Festivals and ''Influential'' members of the community: the case of the Kurayami-matsuri Festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu-shi, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (23), 51-64. *Tsuruga Eisuke 2007 Possibility on recovery of the humanity, concerned with festival reciprocity : Through the Fuchu Kurayami Matsuri researches. ''Education for sustainable development'' 6, 105-112. *Mogi Sakae, Shimada Kiyoshi 1989 The Kurayami Matsuri at Okunitama Shrine in Fuchu ''Transactions of the institute for Japanese culture and classics'' 64, 140-207, *杉浦 翔子 2006 A study of the chief priest system of the plum wine drinking ritual held at Owari-no-Okunitama Jinja 『皇学館論叢』 39(6), 36-63, *Koide Goro 1983 On Argonauta argo Housed in the Okunitama Shrine.『ちりぼたん』 14(1), 21. ===Utagaki=== *糸永 正之 2009 ''Utagaki'' in Bhutan: the verification of face-to-face interaction through fixed-verse songs. ''Asian folk culture studies'' (8), 1-32. *Nittamachi Yoshinao 1997 The Symbolism of The Expression in Touka. ''Research memoirs of the Kobe Technical College'' 35, 89-94. *Miyazaki Takeshi 1997 A Study of a Traditional Event Utagaki in Tsugaru Area.7 『日本歌謡研究』 37, 73-83. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category}} * [http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ Official website] {{in lang|ja}} {{Coord|35|40|02.4|N|139|28|44.4|E|source:jawiki_scale:25000|display=title}} {{Ōtori Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Sōja shrines}} {{draft categories| [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]] [[Category:Fuchū, Tokyo]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] }} [[sn:Ōkunitama Shrine]] [[en:Ōkunitama Shrine]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] {{Commons category|Okunitama-jinja, Fuchu}} [[fa:معبد اوکونیتاما]] [[fr:Ōkunitama-jinja]] [[ja:大國魂神社]] [[zh:大國魂神社]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] {{wikidata link|Q611678}} [[Category:pages with conflicting qids]]

On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. 大國魂神社 | image = File:Ōkunitama Shrine.jpg | caption = Ōkunitama Jinja Haiden | map_type = Japan | map_alt = | coordinates = {{Coord|35.667333|N|139.479|E|region:JP_type:landmark|display=inline,title}} | map_relief = | map_size = | map_caption = | religious_affiliation = [[Shinto]] | type = [[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]] ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Kanpei-shōsha]]) | deity = {{ill|Ōkuninushi|WD=Q276944}} | founded_by = | established = 111 AD (legendary) | date_destroyed = | location = | website = {{URL|http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/}} | architecture_style = {{ill|nagare-zukuri|WD=Q210684}} | festival = | leadership = | prefecture= {{ill|Fuchū|WD=Q208818}} }} {{Nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社|Ōkunitama Jinja}} is a [[:en:Shinto shrine|shrine]] located in [[:en:Fuchū, Tokyo|Fuchū, Tokyo]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]]. Six shrines in [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] were consolidated and their gods enshrined there. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. Ōkunitama is now known as one of the five major shrines in Tokyo, the others being the Tokyo Great Shrine, [[:en:Yasukuni Shrine|Yasukuni Shrine]], [[Hie Shrine]] and [[Meiji Jingu|Meiji Shrine]].{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} It is the [[Sōja shrine|Sōja]] of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] It is dedicated to [[:en:Kunitama|Musahi no Okunitama]] identified as [[Ōkuninushi]] ==General description== [[File:Keyaki Namiki N Cross autumn.jpg|right|thumb|''Keyaki Namiki'' Crossing]] [[File:Fuchuookunitamajinjyakorou.jpg|right|thumb|Drum Tower]] [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.shidarezakura.jpg|right|thumb|The cherry tree beside the hand-washing station]] Within the shrine complex, there are many buildings and points of interest. The main shrine buildings are in a walled inner complex protected by an inner and outer gate. The main shrine is dedicated to [[Ōkuninushi]]. In addition, the main shrine is also an amalgamation of branches of the six main shrines from around Musashi Province: In addition, the main shrine complex is surrounded by seven smaller subsidiary shrines. These are ''Matsuo Shrine'', ''Tatsumi Shrine'', ''Tōshōguu Shrine'', ''Sumiyoshi Shrine'', ''Ōwashi Shrine'', ''Miyanome Shrine'' and an ''[[:en:Inari shrine|Inari shrine]]''. There is also a [[:en:Sumo|Sumo]] ring and a [[:en:Russo-Japanese War|Russo-Japanese War]] memorial, as well as the remains of the former [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi]] provincial office. ==History== According to the shrine's legend, it was established on 5 May in the 41st year of the reign of [[:en:Emperor Keikō|Emperor Keikō]], which corresponds to 111 AD in the western calendar. The offspring of ''Noomiame-no-hohino-mikoto'' (出雲臣天穂日命) appointed ''[[Kuni no miyatsuko]]'' of [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]], the capital of which was located in what is now Fuchū. Its position as the {{nihongo|central shrine|総社|Sosha}} of Musashi Province was confirmed from the [[:en:Taika (era)|Taika period]] (645 AD), and archaeological evidence confirms that the shrine was located very close to the provincial capital (''[[kokufu]]'') of Musashi. During the late [[:en:Heian period|Heian period]] (1062) [[Minamoto no Yoriyoshi]] and his son, [[:en:Minamoto no Yoshiie|Minamoto no Yoshiie]] donated thousands of [[:en:Zelkova|Zelkova]] saplings to the shrine as part of a prayer for victory in military campaigns in [[:en:Mutsu Province|Mutsu Province]], and in 1182 [[Minamoto no Yoritomo]] made an invocation for the safe delivery of a child during the pregnancy of [[:en:Hojo Masako|Hojo Masako]]. Following the start of the [[:en:Kamakura period|Kamakura period]], Minamoto no Yoritomo extensively rebuilt the shrine. It was rebuilt again in 1590 under [[:en:Tokugawa Ieyasu|Tokugawa Ieyasu]] and after a fire in 1649. Under the [[:en:State Shinto|State Shinto]] system of the [[:en:Meiji era|Meiji era]], the shrine was officially renamed Ōkunitama Jinja in 1872, and appointed a Kanpei-shōsha ([[Modern system of Ranked Shinto shrines|Imperial Shrine, 3rd Rank]]) in 1886. [[File:大国魂神社.JPG|thumbnail|Kurayami Festival]] ==Kurayami matsuri== The {{Nihongo|''Kurayami matsuri''|くらやみ祭り|Darkness Festival}} is claimed to be one of the three oldest festivals in [[:en:Kanto region|Kanto region]]. This festival is held every year, between 30 April and 6 May. Originally this festival was described as an {{Nihongo|''[[:en:Utagaki|Utagaki]]''| 歌垣|courtship song festival }}.{{Citation needed|date=September 2010}} [[:en:Ryotaro Shiba|Ryotaro Shiba]], a Japanese essay writer and novelist, observed that this festival resulted in disorderly conduct by the participants.司馬遼太郎1964『燃えよ剣』 He claimed that, amongst the single men and women who had gathered to sing and dance for each other, were also those who were married and who intended to have sex under cover of darkness. In the [[:en:Meiji Era|Meiji Era]], facing criticism from Christian [[:en:Missionary|missionaries]], the authorities put a stop to this festival. In its place, ''Kurayami Matsuri'' was created. ''Kurayami'' means 'darkness' and ''matsuri'' means 'festival' in Japanese. It was originally held during the night, but this was changed to evening in 1959. On May 4, the road approaching the temple ({{Nihongo|''Keyaki Namiki''|ケヤキ並木|Zelkova Row}}) is used as a track for horse-racing and performances of a masked folk dance known as {{Nihongo|''Fuchuu Hayashi''|府中囃子}}. On May 5, six large [[:en:Taiko|taiko drums]] lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships [[:en:Yamato Okunitama|Yamato Okunitama]]) * [[:en:Musashi Province|Musashi Province]] [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (24), 47-60. *中里 亮平 2008 Festivals and ''Influential'' members of the community: the case of the Kurayami-matsuri Festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu-shi, Tokyo. ''The Japanese folklore review'' (23), 51-64. *Tsuruga Eisuke 2007 Possibility on recovery of the humanity, concerned with festival reciprocity : Through the Fuchu Kurayami Matsuri researches. ''Education for sustainable development'' 6, 105-112. *Mogi Sakae, Shimada Kiyoshi 1989 The Kurayami Matsuri at Okunitama Shrine in Fuchu ''Transactions of the institute for Japanese culture and classics'' 64, 140-207, *杉浦 翔子 2006 A study of the chief priest system of the plum wine drinking ritual held at Owari-no-Okunitama Jinja 『皇学館論叢』 39(6), 36-63, *Koide Goro 1983 On Argonauta argo Housed in the Okunitama Shrine.『ちりぼたん』 14(1), 21. ===Utagaki=== *糸永 正之 2009 ''Utagaki'' in Bhutan: the verification of face-to-face interaction through fixed-verse songs. ''Asian folk culture studies'' (8), 1-32. *Nittamachi Yoshinao 1997 The Symbolism of The Expression in Touka. ''Research memoirs of the Kobe Technical College'' 35, 89-94. *Miyazaki Takeshi 1997 A Study of a Traditional Event Utagaki in Tsugaru Area.7 『日本歌謡研究』 37, 73-83. ==References== {{Reflist}} ==External links== {{Commons Category:Pages and Categories from Wikipedia 2]] [[Category}} * [http://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ Official website] {{in lang|ja}} {{Coord|35|40|02.4|N|139|28|44.4|E|source:jawiki_scale:25000|display=title}} {{Ōtori Faith}} {{Beppyo Shrines}} \ {{Sōja shrines}} [[sn:Ōkunitama Shrine]] [[en:Ōkunitama Shrine]] {{Commons category|Okunitama-jinja, Fuchu}} [[fa:معبد اوکونیتاما]] [[fr:Ōkunitama-jinja]] [[ja:大國魂神社]] [[zh:大國魂神社]] {{wikidata link|Q611678}} [[Category:Beppyo shrines]] [[Category:Fuchū, Tokyo]] [[Category:Kanpei Shōsha]] [[Category:Qq]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[Category:Shinto shrines in Tokyo]] [[Category:Sōja shrines]] [[Category:Tokyo Metropolitan Designated Tangible Cultural Property]] [[Category:Wikidata has English label]] [[Category:Wikidata has short description]]

On May 5, six large {{ill|Taiko|en|Taiko|WD=Q221769|lt=taiko drums}} lead eight [[mikoshi]] to a temporary holding area. They are returned to the shrine early in the morning the following day. ==See also== * [[Owari Ōkunitama Shrine]] * [[Ōyamato Shrine]] (worships {{ill|Yamato Okunitama|en|Yamato Okunitama|WD=Q11387080|lt=Yamato Okunitama}}) * {{ill|Musashi Province|en|Musashi Province|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}} [[Ichinomiya]] ** [[Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)]] ** [[Ono Shrine]] ==List of Research papers for== ===Kurayami matsuri and Ohkunitama shrine=== *中里 亮平 2009 Matsuri boom and influence on festivals: the case of the kurayami-matsuri festival at Okunitama shrine in Fuchu, Tokyo.
