{{jalink|別表神社|Q10898274|Beppyo Shrine}} |Founded = (Traditionally) 41st year of Emperor Keikō (12th emperor) |Main Hall = Three-bay nagare-zukuri, copper roofing |Other Name = Rokushō-gū |Affiliation = Tokyo Five Shrines |Main Festival = {{jalink|5月5日|Q2550|May 5}} |Rituals = {{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}} ({{jalink|4月30日|Q2536|April 30}}–{{jalink|5月6日|Q2552|May 6}}) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Tokyo|lat_deg=35|lat_min=40|lat_sec=2.8|lon_deg=139|lon_min=28|lon_sec=44.1|label=Ōkunitama Shrine|position=top|width=180|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} }} [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.ootorii.jpg|thumb|The Great Torii and shrine name pillar]] '''Ōkunitama Shrine''' (おおくにたまじんじゃ; {{smaller|{{jalink|新字体|Q1055887|modern characters}}:}} 大国魂神社) is a {{jalink|神社|Q845945|Shinto shrine}} located in {{jalink|東京都|Q1490|Tokyo Metropolis}}, {{jalink|府中市 (東京都)|Q208818|Fuchū City}}, {{jalink|宮町 (東京都府中市)|Q116980587|Miyamachi}}. It is the {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}} and one of the Tokyo Five Shrines.The other four are {{jalink|東京大神宮|Q11524717|Tokyo Daijingu}}, {{jalink|靖国神社|Q242803|Yasukuni Shrine}}, {{jalink|日枝神社 (千代田区)|Q702042|Hie Shrine}}, and {{jalink|明治神宮|Q287165|Meiji Shrine}}. Because it enshrines together the deities from the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province, it is also known as '''Rokushō-gū''' (“Shrine of Six Deities”). === Overview === [[File:Musashi.kokufu.ato.fuchu.tokyo.jpg|thumb|Historic Site: {{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Ruins of the Musashi Provincial Capital}}]] [[File:Furusato.fuchu.rekishikan.jpg|thumb|Furusato Fuchū History Museum]] In {{jalink|古代|Q41493|ancient times}}, {{jalink|国司|Q1351234|provincial governors}} visited all the shrines in their jurisdiction, starting from the ichinomiya (first shrine). To simplify this long pilgrimage, a {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} was established near each province’s {{jalink|国府|Q1629088|provincial capital}}, where the gods of the province were collectively enshrined. This shrine served as the sōja of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}}. The shrine stands in the center of Fuchū City; the city name “Fuchū” derives from the former location of the Musashi provincial capital. The shrine grounds occupy the site of that capital, while the municipal land to the east across the road is designated a national {{jalink|史跡|Q1081138|historic site}} as the “{{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Musashi Provincial Capital Ruins}} (Musashi Government Office Area).” This eastern area has been developed with marked pillar sites and exhibition rooms, and includes the Furusato Fuchū History Museum. The shrine is also near the center of {{jalink|府中宿 (甲州街道)|Q11486027|Fuchū Post Town}}, and a road once connected the Great Torii to {{jalink|武蔵国分寺跡|Q11546338|Musashi Kokubunji}} and the Musashi {{jalink|国分尼寺|Q131908135|Kokubunniji}}. According to tradition, the shrine was founded on May 5, 111 CE, in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the provincial capital was established here during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140|Taika Reforms}}. Legends recount that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Minamoto no Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory before campaigns in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Mutsu Province}}, and that their descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800|Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830|wife}}. The grounds contain many shrine buildings and numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846|komainu}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622|Important Cultural Properties}}. Despite its location in the city center near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794|Fuchū-Hommachi Station}}, the shrine is surrounded by trees, and the {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|Baba-Daimon Zelkova Avenue}} along the approach is designated a national Natural Monument. The shrine’s main festival is the '''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}}''', designated a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and counted among the three great “strange festivals” of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841|Kantō}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The main hall enshrines the following deities. As the sōja of Musashi Province, it enshrines together the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi (collectively known as the Bushū Rokusha Myōjin). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' – Principal deity; identified with {{jalink|大国主神|Ōkuninushi}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263|Tama City}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480|Akiruno City}}, Tokyo)Although this shrine enshrines Ninomiya Shrine as the second shrine at the time of its founding, historically there is also a theory that {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} was the second shrine. * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633|Hikawa Shrine}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186|Saitama Prefecture}}, {{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635|Saitama City}}, {{jalink|大宮区|Q153629|Ōmiya Ward}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366|Chichibu Shrine}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079|Chichibu City}}, Saitama) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038|Kodama District}}, {{jalink|神川町|Q1346757|Kamikawa Town}}, Saitama) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513|Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{jalink|横浜市|Q38283|Yokohama}}, {{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})Multiple shrines claim to be the Sixth Shrine of Musashi. It is said that in the early years, Shinto priests from across Musashi gathered on the founding date, May 5, to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637|Illustrated Famous Places of Edo}}: Fuchū Rokushō-gū]] === Founding === According to shrine traditions such as the *Fuchū Rokushō-sha Den*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the local people enshrined him. Descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命|Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto}}, ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏|Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造|Musashi no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and served the shrine for generations. The founding of the shrine is traditionally said to date to the 41st year of Emperor Keikō (May 5, 111 CE), and it is said that during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}} the provincial government was placed at its present location. Traditions remain that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory when heading to the wars in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Ōshū}}, and that their direct descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} also prayed here for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830}}. The precincts consist of many shrine buildings and preserve numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622}}. Although it is located in the center of the city near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794}}, it is surrounded by trees, and the approach lined with zelkova trees known as {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}} is designated a National Natural Monument. The shrine’s {{jalink|例大祭}} is the “'''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601}}''',” which is designated as a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and is counted as one of the three great {{jalink|奇祭|Q11444891}} of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The deities enshrined in the main hall are as follows. As the general shrine of Musashi Province, it enshrines the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province at the time of its founding (commonly called the Six Shrines of Bushū). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' (おおくにたまのおおかみ) – Principal deity. Considered identical to {{jalink|大国主神}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480}}, Tokyo)At this shrine, Ninomiya Shrine is enshrined as the Second Shrine at the time of the founding; however, historically there is also a theory that the Fifth Shrine, Kanzan Shrine, was considered the Second Shrine (see “{{jalink|一宮#諸国一宮一覧|Q1656379}}”). * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186}}{{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635}}{{jalink|大宮区|Q153629}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038}}{{jalink|神川町|Q1346757}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513}}{{jalink|横浜市|Q38283}}{{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})This shrine regards the Sugiyama Shrine in Nishihassaku-chō, Midori Ward, as the Sixth Shrine, but there are multiple claimant shrines for the Sixth Shrine of Musashi Province (see “{{jalink|杉山神社|Q135039726}}”). In the early period after its establishment, it is said that on the founding date of May 5, priests from all over Musashi Province gathered to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637}} Fuchū Rokusho Shrine]] === Founding === According to traditions recorded in shrine records such as *Fuchū Rokusho Shrine Tradition*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of Emperor Keikō, and the local people enshrined the deity, forming the origin of the shrine. Thereafter, descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命}}, the ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏||Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造}} and served the shrine; successive provincial rulers performed the rites and administration of worship{{cite book|和書| author=Tokyo Prefecture (ed.)| title=Tokyo Prefecture Nishitama District, Minamitama District, Kitatama District Guide to Famous Places, Historic Sites, and Products| chapter=Ōkunitama Shrine| year=1912| publisher=Tokyo Prefecture| pages=pp. 92f| url={{NDLDC|946884/117}}}}. At that time, the shrine was called “Ōkunitama Shrine.” === Overview === * {{jalink|大化|Q1077930}} 1 ({{jalink|645年|Q31040}}) – During the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}}, the provincial capital of Musashi was placed within the precincts, and the shrine became the ritual site of the provincial government, with the governor overseeing the rites of the province. Deities of the province were enshrined for the convenience of offerings and rituals, forming the origin of the Musashi General Shrine. At this time, the name became “Musashi General Shrine,” and later, with the enshrinement of six notable deities of Musashi Province, it became “Musashi General Shrine Rokusho-no-miya.” * {{jalink|康平|Q1193572}} 5 (1062) – During the pacification of the {{jalink|前九年の役|Q1187448}}, {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} donated one thousand saplings of {{jalink|ケヤキ|Q920344|zelkova}}. This became the origin of the present {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}}, now a National {{jalink|天然記念物|Q23790}}. Also, because {{jalink|スモモ|Q1250033|plums}} were offered as {{jalink|供物|Q12682000}}, the annual “Plum Festival” came to be held on {{jalink|7月20日|Q2728}}. * {{jalink|寿永|Q598057}} 1 (1182) – {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} sent {{jalink|葛西清重|Q11621006|Kassai Saburō Kiyoshige}} as an envoy to pray for the safe childbirth of {{jalink|北条政子|Q463961|Masako}}. * {{jalink|文治|Q1194415}} 2 (1186) – Yoritomo appointed {{jalink|平賀義信|Q11483573|Hiraga Yoshinobu}} as {{jalink|奉行|Q2535820}} to construct shrine buildings. * {{jalink|貞永|Q1194168}} 1, 2nd month (1232) – Repairs were carried out under {{jalink|北条泰時|Q1188359}}, the third {{jalink|執権|Q1045904}} of the {{jalink|鎌倉幕府|Q736839}}. * {{jalink|天正|Q1145058}} 18 (1590), 8th month – After {{jalink|徳川家康|Q171977}} entered Edo, 500 koku of shrine lands were donated as the general shrine of Musashi Province, and buildings were constructed. * {{jalink|正保|Q1146192}} 3 (1646), 10th month – Shrine buildings were destroyed by fire. * {{jalink|寛文|Q1146228}} 7 (1667) – By order of {{jalink|徳川家綱|Q323422}}, {{jalink|久世広之|Q10859992|Kuze Yamato-no-kami Hiroyuki}} rebuilt the shrine buildings, which remain today. During the {{jalink|慶応|Q776775|Keiō era}} (mid-19th century), the {{jalink|檜皮葺|Q90373477}} roofing was changed to copper plate roofing. * {{jalink|文久|Q730266}} 1 (1861) – A commemorative match was held celebrating the succession of {{jalink|近藤勇|Q467334}} as the fourth head of {{jalink|天然理心流|Q1445791}}, later commander of the {{jalink|新選組|Q221031}}. * {{jalink|明治|Q3125096}} 1 ({{jalink|1868年|Q7717}}) – Ranked equivalent to a {{jalink|勅祭社|Q175288}}. * Meiji 4 ({{jalink|1871年|Q7746}}) – Renamed “Ōkunitama Shrine.” * {{jalink|1875年|Q7764}} (Meiji 7) – Classified as a prefectural shrine under the {{jalink|近代社格制度|Q712534}}. * {{jalink|1886年|Q7822}} (Meiji 18) – Classified as a {{jalink|近代社格制度#官社|Q712534|Kanpei Shōsha}}. * {{jalink|2011年|Q1994}} ({{jalink|平成|Q234510}} 23) – New construction of the purification hall, renovation of the Zuishin Gate, and relocation of the handwashing pavilion. * {{jalink|2017年|Q25290}} (Heisei 29) – Construction of the west approach and torii gate. === Grounds === According to the saying of the enshrined deity, “pines bring sorrow—only cedars,” no pine trees are planted within the shrine grounds. As a result, in the local city of Fuchū, it is common to use “gate bamboo” instead of pine for New Year’s {{jalink|kadomatsu|Q2667233}}. The main sanctuary is built in the style of one structure with three sanctuaries, finished entirely in vermilion lacquer and roofed with copper plates. It was constructed in Kanbun 7 (1667) during the Edo period, changing from the earlier three-structure, three-sanctuary form to its current configuration. It is designated a cultural property of Tokyo Metropolis. The {{jalink|otabisho|Q11489117}} is located at the “Fuchū City Hall Front” intersection ({{Coord|35|40|11.45|N|139|28|35.64|E|region:JP-13|name=Otobisho}}), and during the annual festival the portable shrines are carried there. Adjacent to it remains the takafuda notice board of {{jalink|Fuchū-shuku (Kōshū Kaidō)|Q11486027|Fuchū-shuku}} (a Tokyo-designated cultural property). In addition, behind the Suijinsha within the grounds there is a place where the ritual of “hitogata nagashi” is performed, in which paper effigies are rubbed on the body and then floated down a river to cleanse impurity.[https://www.city.fuchu.tokyo.jp/kirari/sagasu/theme/jiman/ookunitamajinja_keidai.html Ōkunitama Shrine Grounds] Fuchū City official website (viewed January 21, 2018) Elsewhere on the grounds are a shrine office for amulets, waiting hall, kagura hall, treasure hall, {{jalink|temizuya}}, cloister, {{jalink|shamusho}}, {{jalink|wedding hall|Q7979077}}, war memorial, {{jalink|Russo-Japanese War|Q159950|Russo-Japanese War}} memorial, memorial monument to the fallen of the cruiser Tama, and a {{jalink|sumo|Q40561}} ring. Among these, the former Imperial Japanese Navy {{jalink|Tama (light cruiser)|Q1817205|light cruiser Tama}} had Ōkunitama Shrine as its shipboard shrine; since October 25, 2014—70 years after its sinking—a memorial service has been held every year on the same date.[https://www.sankei.com/article/20171026-LBSXU2ML7ZLOFK36VSPEGHFQHA/ “May the cruiser Tama rest in peace: 100 attend memorial at Ōkunitama Shrine”] *Sankei Shimbun*, morning edition, October 26, 2017 (Tokyo) The entire precinct is non-smoking and bicycle riding is prohibited; however, during the {{jalink|2020 Tokyo Olympics cycling events|Q39080749}}, the road race parade route passed through the grounds,[https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/wp/info/2697.html Notice of traffic restrictions for Tokyo Olympics cycling road race (7/24–25)] Ōkunitama Shrine official website (viewed July 27, 2021) and many athletes rode their bicycles through the approach. === Gallery === {{Gallery |align=center |width=160 |height=120 15|Q2774}} === Approach === The approach is lined with {{jalink|zelkova trees|Q920344|keyaki}}. This is said to date back to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, as well as Tokugawa Ieyasu. The “Keyaki Namiki Avenue,” officially known as the “Baba Daimon Zelkova Avenue,” stretches to the northern intersection before the Tokyo Metropolitan Agricultural High School and was designated Japan’s second natural monument in 1924—the only zelkova avenue so designated in the country. === Festivals === Nearly 400 rituals are held annually, including the daily offerings to the deities. Since 2018, the New Year’s bonfire rite {{jalink|Sagichō|Q9332740}} has newly been performed as a Shinto ceremony. === Annual Festival Calendar === *(table omitted for brevity; structure and dates unchanged)* === Grand Festival (Kurayami Festival) === The grand festival of Ōkunitama Shrine is the {{jalink|Kurayami Festival}}, one of the three great unusual festivals of the Kantō region. Held annually from April 30 to May 6, it originally had the character of {{jalink|utagaki|Q610915}}, though its more licentious customs were reformed in the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} era. === Cultural Properties === *(sections translated as titled; designations and dates unchanged)* === Access Information === * Address: Miyamachi 3-1, {{jalink|Fuchū City (Tokyo)|Q208818}}, {{jalink|Tokyo Metropolis|Q1490}} * Nearest stations: * JR East {{jalink|Nambu Line|Q1366263}} / {{jalink|Musashino Line|Q1191671}} {{jalink|Fuchū-Hommachi Station|Q800794}} (2 min walk) * {{jalink|Keio Line|Q1323112}} {{jalink|Fuchū Station (Tokyo)|Q4493756}} or {{jalink|Keio Keibajō Line|Q656122}} {{jalink|Fuchū Keiba-Seimonmae Station|Q4493753}} (5 min walk) === External Links === * Official website: https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:Shikinaisha]] [[Category:Shinto shrine]] [[Category:Shikinai Ronsha]] [[Category:Kokuhei-sha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Musashi Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:東京都の神社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:官幣小社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:准勅祭社]] [[Category:東京都府中市の歴史]] [[Category:東京都府中市の建築物]] [[Category:武蔵国|社0]] [[Category:東京都の重要文化財]] [[Category:東京都指定有形文化財]] [[Category:東京都内の区市町村指定有形文化財]] [[Category:江戸時代の建築]]

{{jalink|別表神社|Q10898274|Beppyo Shrine}} |Founded = (Traditionally) 41st year of Emperor Keikō (12th emperor) |Main Hall = Three-bay nagare-zukuri, copper roofing |Other Name = Rokushō-gū |Affiliation = Tokyo Five Shrines |Main Festival = {{jalink|5月5日|Q2550|May 5}} |Rituals = {{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}} ({{jalink|4月30日|Q2536|April 30}}–{{jalink|5月6日|Q2552|May 6}}) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Tokyo|lat_deg=35|lat_min=40|lat_sec=2.8|lon_deg=139|lon_min=28|lon_sec=44.1|label=Ōkunitama Shrine|position=top|width=180|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} }} [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.ootorii.jpg|thumb|The Great Torii and shrine name pillar]] '''Ōkunitama Shrine''' (おおくにたまじんじゃ; {{smaller|{{jalink|新字体|Q1055887|modern characters}}:}} 大国魂神社) is a {{jalink|神社|Q845945|Shinto shrine}} located in {{jalink|東京都|Q1490|Tokyo Metropolis}}, {{jalink|府中市 (東京都)|Q208818|Fuchū City}}, {{jalink|宮町 (東京都府中市)|Q116980587|Miyamachi}}. It is the {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}} and one of the Tokyo Five Shrines.The other four are {{jalink|東京大神宮|Q11524717|Tokyo Daijingu}}, {{jalink|靖国神社|Q242803|Yasukuni Shrine}}, {{jalink|日枝神社 (千代田区)|Q702042|Hie Shrine}}, and {{jalink|明治神宮|Q287165|Meiji Shrine}}. Because it enshrines together the deities from the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province, it is also known as '''Rokushō-gū''' (“Shrine of Six Deities”). === Overview === [[File:Musashi.kokufu.ato.fuchu.tokyo.jpg|thumb|Historic Site: {{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Ruins of the Musashi Provincial Capital}}]] [[File:Furusato.fuchu.rekishikan.jpg|thumb|Furusato Fuchū History Museum]] In {{jalink|古代|Q41493|ancient times}}, {{jalink|国司|Q1351234|provincial governors}} visited all the shrines in their jurisdiction, starting from the ichinomiya (first shrine). To simplify this long pilgrimage, a {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} was established near each province’s {{jalink|国府|Q1629088|provincial capital}}, where the gods of the province were collectively enshrined. This shrine served as the sōja of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}}. The shrine stands in the center of Fuchū City; the city name “Fuchū” derives from the former location of the Musashi provincial capital. The shrine grounds occupy the site of that capital, while the municipal land to the east across the road is designated a national {{jalink|史跡|Q1081138|historic site}} as the “{{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Musashi Provincial Capital Ruins}} (Musashi Government Office Area).” This eastern area has been developed with marked pillar sites and exhibition rooms, and includes the Furusato Fuchū History Museum. The shrine is also near the center of {{jalink|府中宿 (甲州街道)|Q11486027|Fuchū Post Town}}, and a road once connected the Great Torii to {{jalink|武蔵国分寺跡|Q11546338|Musashi Kokubunji}} and the Musashi {{jalink|国分尼寺|Q131908135|Kokubunniji}}. According to tradition, the shrine was founded on May 5, 111 CE, in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the provincial capital was established here during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140|Taika Reforms}}. Legends recount that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Minamoto no Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory before campaigns in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Mutsu Province}}, and that their descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800|Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830|wife}}. The grounds contain many shrine buildings and numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846|komainu}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622|Important Cultural Properties}}. Despite its location in the city center near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794|Fuchū-Hommachi Station}}, the shrine is surrounded by trees, and the {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|Baba-Daimon Zelkova Avenue}} along the approach is designated a national Natural Monument. The shrine’s main festival is the '''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}}''', designated a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and counted among the three great “strange festivals” of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841|Kantō}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The main hall enshrines the following deities. As the sōja of Musashi Province, it enshrines together the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi (collectively known as the Bushū Rokusha Myōjin). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' – Principal deity; identified with {{jalink|大国主神|Ōkuninushi}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263|Tama City}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480|Akiruno City}}, Tokyo)Although this shrine enshrines Ninomiya Shrine as the second shrine at the time of its founding, historically there is also a theory that {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} was the second shrine. * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633|Hikawa Shrine}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186|Saitama Prefecture}}, {{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635|Saitama City}}, {{jalink|大宮区|Q153629|Ōmiya Ward}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366|Chichibu Shrine}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079|Chichibu City}}, Saitama) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038|Kodama District}}, {{jalink|神川町|Q1346757|Kamikawa Town}}, Saitama) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513|Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{jalink|横浜市|Q38283|Yokohama}}, {{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})Multiple shrines claim to be the Sixth Shrine of Musashi. It is said that in the early years, Shinto priests from across Musashi gathered on the founding date, May 5, to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637|Illustrated Famous Places of Edo}}: Fuchū Rokushō-gū]] === Founding === According to shrine traditions such as the *Fuchū Rokushō-sha Den*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the local people enshrined him. Descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命|Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto}}, ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏|Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造|Musashi no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and served the shrine for generations. The founding of the shrine is traditionally said to date to the 41st year of Emperor Keikō (May 5, 111 CE), and it is said that during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}} the provincial government was placed at its present location. Traditions remain that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory when heading to the wars in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Ōshū}}, and that their direct descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} also prayed here for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830}}. The precincts consist of many shrine buildings and preserve numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622}}. Although it is located in the center of the city near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794}}, it is surrounded by trees, and the approach lined with zelkova trees known as {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}} is designated a National Natural Monument. The shrine’s {{jalink|例大祭}} is the “'''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601}}''',” which is designated as a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and is counted as one of the three great {{jalink|奇祭|Q11444891}} of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The deities enshrined in the main hall are as follows. As the general shrine of Musashi Province, it enshrines the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province at the time of its founding (commonly called the Six Shrines of Bushū). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' (おおくにたまのおおかみ) – Principal deity. Considered identical to {{jalink|大国主神}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480}}, Tokyo)At this shrine, Ninomiya Shrine is enshrined as the Second Shrine at the time of the founding; however, historically there is also a theory that the Fifth Shrine, Kanzan Shrine, was considered the Second Shrine (see “{{jalink|一宮#諸国一宮一覧|Q1656379}}”). * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186}}{{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635}}{{jalink|大宮区|Q153629}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038}}{{jalink|神川町|Q1346757}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513}}{{jalink|横浜市|Q38283}}{{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})This shrine regards the Sugiyama Shrine in Nishihassaku-chō, Midori Ward, as the Sixth Shrine, but there are multiple claimant shrines for the Sixth Shrine of Musashi Province (see “{{jalink|杉山神社|Q135039726}}”). In the early period after its establishment, it is said that on the founding date of May 5, priests from all over Musashi Province gathered to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637}} Fuchū Rokusho Shrine]] === Founding === According to traditions recorded in shrine records such as *Fuchū Rokusho Shrine Tradition*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of Emperor Keikō, and the local people enshrined the deity, forming the origin of the shrine. Thereafter, descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命}}, the ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏||Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造}} and served the shrine; successive provincial rulers performed the rites and administration of worship{{cite book|和書| author=Tokyo Prefecture (ed.)| title=Tokyo Prefecture Nishitama District, Minamitama District, Kitatama District Guide to Famous Places, Historic Sites, and Products| chapter=Ōkunitama Shrine| year=1912| publisher=Tokyo Prefecture| pages=pp. 92f| url={{NDLDC|946884/117}}}}. At that time, the shrine was called “Ōkunitama Shrine.” === Overview === * {{jalink|大化|Q1077930}} 1 ({{jalink|645年|Q31040}}) – During the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}}, the provincial capital of Musashi was placed within the precincts, and the shrine became the ritual site of the provincial government, with the governor overseeing the rites of the province. Deities of the province were enshrined for the convenience of offerings and rituals, forming the origin of the Musashi General Shrine. At this time, the name became “Musashi General Shrine,” and later, with the enshrinement of six notable deities of Musashi Province, it became “Musashi General Shrine Rokusho-no-miya.” * {{jalink|康平|Q1193572}} 5 (1062) – During the pacification of the {{jalink|前九年の役|Q1187448}}, {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} donated one thousand saplings of {{jalink|ケヤキ|Q920344|zelkova}}. This became the origin of the present {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}}, now a National {{jalink|天然記念物|Q23790}}. Also, because {{jalink|スモモ|Q1250033|plums}} were offered as {{jalink|供物|Q12682000}}, the annual “Plum Festival” came to be held on {{jalink|7月20日|Q2728}}. * {{jalink|寿永|Q598057}} 1 (1182) – {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} sent {{jalink|葛西清重|Q11621006|Kassai Saburō Kiyoshige}} as an envoy to pray for the safe childbirth of {{jalink|北条政子|Q463961|Masako}}. * {{jalink|文治|Q1194415}} 2 (1186) – Yoritomo appointed {{jalink|平賀義信|Q11483573|Hiraga Yoshinobu}} as {{jalink|奉行|Q2535820}} to construct shrine buildings. * {{jalink|貞永|Q1194168}} 1, 2nd month (1232) – Repairs were carried out under {{jalink|北条泰時|Q1188359}}, the third {{jalink|執権|Q1045904}} of the {{jalink|鎌倉幕府|Q736839}}. * {{jalink|天正|Q1145058}} 18 (1590), 8th month – After {{jalink|徳川家康|Q171977}} entered Edo, 500 koku of shrine lands were donated as the general shrine of Musashi Province, and buildings were constructed. * {{jalink|正保|Q1146192}} 3 (1646), 10th month – Shrine buildings were destroyed by fire. * {{jalink|寛文|Q1146228}} 7 (1667) – By order of {{jalink|徳川家綱|Q323422}}, {{jalink|久世広之|Q10859992|Kuze Yamato-no-kami Hiroyuki}} rebuilt the shrine buildings, which remain today. During the {{jalink|慶応|Q776775|Keiō era}} (mid-19th century), the {{jalink|檜皮葺|Q90373477}} roofing was changed to copper plate roofing. * {{jalink|文久|Q730266}} 1 (1861) – A commemorative match was held celebrating the succession of {{jalink|近藤勇|Q467334}} as the fourth head of {{jalink|天然理心流|Q1445791}}, later commander of the {{jalink|新選組|Q221031}}. * {{jalink|明治|Q3125096}} 1 ({{jalink|1868年|Q7717}}) – Ranked equivalent to a {{jalink|勅祭社|Q175288}}. * Meiji 4 ({{jalink|1871年|Q7746}}) – Renamed “Ōkunitama Shrine.” * {{jalink|1875年|Q7764}} (Meiji 7) – Classified as a prefectural shrine under the {{jalink|近代社格制度|Q712534}}. * {{jalink|1886年|Q7822}} (Meiji 18) – Classified as a {{jalink|近代社格制度#官社|Q712534|Kanpei Shōsha}}. * {{jalink|2011年|Q1994}} ({{jalink|平成|Q234510}} 23) – New construction of the purification hall, renovation of the Zuishin Gate, and relocation of the handwashing pavilion. * {{jalink|2017年|Q25290}} (Heisei 29) – Construction of the west approach and torii gate. === Grounds === According to the saying of the enshrined deity, “pines bring sorrow—only cedars,” no pine trees are planted within the shrine grounds. As a result, in the local city of Fuchū, it is common to use “gate bamboo” instead of pine for New Year’s {{jalink|kadomatsu|Q2667233}}. The main sanctuary is built in the style of one structure with three sanctuaries, finished entirely in vermilion lacquer and roofed with copper plates. It was constructed in Kanbun 7 (1667) during the Edo period, changing from the earlier three-structure, three-sanctuary form to its current configuration. It is designated a cultural property of Tokyo Metropolis. The {{jalink|otabisho|Q11489117}} is located at the “Fuchū City Hall Front” intersection ({{Coord|35|40|11.45|N|139|28|35.64|E|region:JP-13|name=Otobisho}}), and during the annual festival the portable shrines are carried there. Adjacent to it remains the takafuda notice board of {{jalink|Fuchū-shuku (Kōshū Kaidō)|Q11486027|Fuchū-shuku}} (a Tokyo-designated cultural property). In addition, behind the Suijinsha within the grounds there is a place where the ritual of “hitogata nagashi” is performed, in which paper effigies are rubbed on the body and then floated down a river to cleanse impurity.[https://www.city.fuchu.tokyo.jp/kirari/sagasu/theme/jiman/ookunitamajinja_keidai.html Ōkunitama Shrine Grounds] Fuchū City official website (viewed January 21, 2018) Elsewhere on the grounds are a shrine office for amulets, waiting hall, kagura hall, treasure hall, {{jalink|temizuya}}, cloister, {{jalink|shamusho}}, {{jalink|wedding hall|Q7979077}}, war memorial, {{jalink|Russo-Japanese War|Q159950|Russo-Japanese War}} memorial, memorial monument to the fallen of the cruiser Tama, and a {{jalink|sumo|Q40561}} ring. Among these, the former Imperial Japanese Navy {{jalink|Tama (light cruiser)|Q1817205|light cruiser Tama}} had Ōkunitama Shrine as its shipboard shrine; since October 25, 2014—70 years after its sinking—a memorial service has been held every year on the same date.[https://www.sankei.com/article/20171026-LBSXU2ML7ZLOFK36VSPEGHFQHA/ “May the cruiser Tama rest in peace: 100 attend memorial at Ōkunitama Shrine”] *Sankei Shimbun*, morning edition, October 26, 2017 (Tokyo) The entire precinct is non-smoking and bicycle riding is prohibited; however, during the {{jalink|2020 Tokyo Olympics cycling events|Q39080749}}, the road race parade route passed through the grounds,[https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/wp/info/2697.html Notice of traffic restrictions for Tokyo Olympics cycling road race (7/24–25)] Ōkunitama Shrine official website (viewed July 27, 2021) and many athletes rode their bicycles through the approach. === Gallery === {{Gallery |align=center |width=160 |height=120 15|Q2774}} === Approach === The approach is lined with {{jalink|zelkova trees|Q920344|keyaki}}. This is said to date back to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, as well as Tokugawa Ieyasu. The “Keyaki Namiki Avenue,” officially known as the “Baba Daimon Zelkova Avenue,” stretches to the northern intersection before the Tokyo Metropolitan Agricultural High School and was designated Japan’s second natural monument in 1924—the only zelkova avenue so designated in the country. === Festivals === Nearly 400 rituals are held annually, including the daily offerings to the deities. Since 2018, the New Year’s bonfire rite {{jalink|Sagichō|Q9332740}} has newly been performed as a Shinto ceremony. === Annual Festival Calendar === *(table omitted for brevity; structure and dates unchanged)* === Grand Festival (Kurayami Festival) === The grand festival of Ōkunitama Shrine is the {{jalink|Kurayami Festival}}, one of the three great unusual festivals of the Kantō region. Held annually from April 30 to May 6, it originally had the character of {{jalink|utagaki|Q610915}}, though its more licentious customs were reformed in the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} era. === Cultural Properties === *(sections translated as titled; designations and dates unchanged)* === Access Information === * Address: Miyamachi 3-1, {{jalink|Fuchū City (Tokyo)|Q208818}}, {{jalink|Tokyo Metropolis|Q1490}} * Nearest stations: * JR East {{jalink|Nambu Line|Q1366263}} / {{jalink|Musashino Line|Q1191671}} {{jalink|Fuchū-Hommachi Station|Q800794}} (2 min walk) * {{jalink|Keio Line|Q1323112}} {{jalink|Fuchū Station (Tokyo)|Q4493756}} or {{jalink|Keio Keibajō Line|Q656122}} {{jalink|Fuchū Keiba-Seimonmae Station|Q4493753}} (5 min walk) === External Links === * Official website: https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:Pages]] [[Category:Shinto shrine]] [[Category:Shikinai Ronsha]] [[Category:Kokuhei-sha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Musashi Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:東京都の神社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:官幣小社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:准勅祭社]] [[Category:東京都府中市の歴史]] [[Category:東京都府中市の建築物]] [[Category:武蔵国|社0]] [[Category:東京都の重要文化財]] [[Category:東京都指定有形文化財]] [[Category:東京都内の区市町村指定有形文化財]] [[Category:江戸時代の建築]]

{{jalink|別表神社|Q10898274|Beppyo Shrine}} |Founded = (Traditionally) 41st year of Emperor Keikō (12th emperor) |Main Hall = Three-bay nagare-zukuri, copper roofing |Other Name = Rokushō-gū |Affiliation = Tokyo Five Shrines |Main Festival = {{jalink|5月5日|Q2550|May 5}} |Rituals = {{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}} ({{jalink|4月30日|Q2536|April 30}}–{{jalink|5月6日|Q2552|May 6}}) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Tokyo|lat_deg=35|lat_min=40|lat_sec=2.8|lon_deg=139|lon_min=28|lon_sec=44.1|label=Ōkunitama Shrine|position=top|width=180|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} }} [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.ootorii.jpg|thumb|The Great Torii and shrine name pillar]] '''Ōkunitama Shrine''' (おおくにたまじんじゃ; {{smaller|{{jalink|新字体|Q1055887|modern characters}}:}} 大国魂神社) is a {{jalink|神社|Q845945|Shinto shrine}} located in {{jalink|東京都|Q1490|Tokyo Metropolis}}, {{jalink|府中市 (東京都)|Q208818|Fuchū City}}, {{jalink|宮町 (東京都府中市)|Q116980587|Miyamachi}}. It is the {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}} and one of the Tokyo Five Shrines.The other four are {{jalink|東京大神宮|Q11524717|Tokyo Daijingu}}, {{jalink|靖国神社|Q242803|Yasukuni Shrine}}, {{jalink|日枝神社 (千代田区)|Q702042|Hie Shrine}}, and {{jalink|明治神宮|Q287165|Meiji Shrine}}. Because it enshrines together the deities from the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province, it is also known as '''Rokushō-gū''' (“Shrine of Six Deities”). === Overview === [[File:Musashi.kokufu.ato.fuchu.tokyo.jpg|thumb|Historic Site: {{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Ruins of the Musashi Provincial Capital}}]] [[File:Furusato.fuchu.rekishikan.jpg|thumb|Furusato Fuchū History Museum]] In {{jalink|古代|Q41493|ancient times}}, {{jalink|国司|Q1351234|provincial governors}} visited all the shrines in their jurisdiction, starting from the ichinomiya (first shrine). To simplify this long pilgrimage, a {{jalink|総社|Q1107129|sōja}} was established near each province’s {{jalink|国府|Q1629088|provincial capital}}, where the gods of the province were collectively enshrined. This shrine served as the sōja of {{jalink|武蔵国|Q907398|Musashi Province}}. The shrine stands in the center of Fuchū City; the city name “Fuchū” derives from the former location of the Musashi provincial capital. The shrine grounds occupy the site of that capital, while the municipal land to the east across the road is designated a national {{jalink|史跡|Q1081138|historic site}} as the “{{jalink|武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|Musashi Provincial Capital Ruins}} (Musashi Government Office Area).” This eastern area has been developed with marked pillar sites and exhibition rooms, and includes the Furusato Fuchū History Museum. The shrine is also near the center of {{jalink|府中宿 (甲州街道)|Q11486027|Fuchū Post Town}}, and a road once connected the Great Torii to {{jalink|武蔵国分寺跡|Q11546338|Musashi Kokubunji}} and the Musashi {{jalink|国分尼寺|Q131908135|Kokubunniji}}. According to tradition, the shrine was founded on May 5, 111 CE, in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the provincial capital was established here during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140|Taika Reforms}}. Legends recount that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Minamoto no Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory before campaigns in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Mutsu Province}}, and that their descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800|Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830|wife}}. The grounds contain many shrine buildings and numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846|komainu}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622|Important Cultural Properties}}. Despite its location in the city center near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794|Fuchū-Hommachi Station}}, the shrine is surrounded by trees, and the {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|Baba-Daimon Zelkova Avenue}} along the approach is designated a national Natural Monument. The shrine’s main festival is the '''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601|Kurayami Festival}}''', designated a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and counted among the three great “strange festivals” of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841|Kantō}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The main hall enshrines the following deities. As the sōja of Musashi Province, it enshrines together the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi (collectively known as the Bushū Rokusha Myōjin). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' – Principal deity; identified with {{jalink|大国主神|Ōkuninushi}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263|Tama City}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480|Akiruno City}}, Tokyo)Although this shrine enshrines Ninomiya Shrine as the second shrine at the time of its founding, historically there is also a theory that {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} was the second shrine. * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633|Hikawa Shrine}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186|Saitama Prefecture}}, {{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635|Saitama City}}, {{jalink|大宮区|Q153629|Ōmiya Ward}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366|Chichibu Shrine}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079|Chichibu City}}, Saitama) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974|Kanayama Shrine}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038|Kodama District}}, {{jalink|神川町|Q1346757|Kamikawa Town}}, Saitama) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513|Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{jalink|横浜市|Q38283|Yokohama}}, {{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})Multiple shrines claim to be the Sixth Shrine of Musashi. It is said that in the early years, Shinto priests from across Musashi gathered on the founding date, May 5, to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637|Illustrated Famous Places of Edo}}: Fuchū Rokushō-gū]] === Founding === According to shrine traditions such as the *Fuchū Rokushō-sha Den*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of {{jalink|景行天皇|Q329723|Emperor Keikō}}, and the local people enshrined him. Descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命|Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto}}, ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏|Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造|Musashi no Kuni no Miyatsuko}} and served the shrine for generations. The founding of the shrine is traditionally said to date to the 41st year of Emperor Keikō (May 5, 111 CE), and it is said that during the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}} the provincial government was placed at its present location. Traditions remain that {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory when heading to the wars in {{jalink|陸奥国|Q907389|Ōshū}}, and that their direct descendant {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} also prayed here for the safe childbirth of his {{jalink|妻|Q188830}}. The precincts consist of many shrine buildings and preserve numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{jalink|狛犬|Q20155846}} designated as {{jalink|重要文化財|Q1188622}}. Although it is located in the center of the city near {{jalink|府中本町駅|Q800794}}, it is surrounded by trees, and the approach lined with zelkova trees known as {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}} is designated a National Natural Monument. The shrine’s {{jalink|例大祭}} is the “'''{{jalink|くらやみ祭|Q11265601}}''',” which is designated as a {{jalink|東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and is counted as one of the three great {{jalink|奇祭|Q11444891}} of the {{jalink|関東|Q11655841}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The deities enshrined in the main hall are as follows. As the general shrine of Musashi Province, it enshrines the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province at the time of its founding (commonly called the Six Shrines of Bushū). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' (おおくにたまのおおかみ) – Principal deity. Considered identical to {{jalink|大国主神}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{jalink|小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|Ono Shrine}} ({{jalink|多摩市|Q213263}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{jalink|二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{jalink|あきる野市|Q240480}}, Tokyo)At this shrine, Ninomiya Shrine is enshrined as the Second Shrine at the time of the founding; however, historically there is also a theory that the Fifth Shrine, Kanzan Shrine, was considered the Second Shrine (see “{{jalink|一宮#諸国一宮一覧|Q1656379}}”). * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{jalink|氷川神社|Q703633}} ({{jalink|埼玉県|Q128186}}{{jalink|さいたま市|Q134635}}{{jalink|大宮区|Q153629}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{jalink|秩父神社|Q2963366}} ({{jalink|秩父市|Q647079}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{jalink|金鑚神社|Q11647974}} ({{jalink|児玉郡|Q938038}}{{jalink|神川町|Q1346757}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{jalink|杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{jalink|神奈川県|Q127513}}{{jalink|横浜市|Q38283}}{{jalink|緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|Midori Ward}})This shrine regards the Sugiyama Shrine in Nishihassaku-chō, Midori Ward, as the Sixth Shrine, but there are multiple claimant shrines for the Sixth Shrine of Musashi Province (see “{{jalink|杉山神社|Q135039726}}”). In the early period after its establishment, it is said that on the founding date of May 5, priests from all over Musashi Province gathered to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{jalink|江戸名所図会|Q2704637}} Fuchū Rokusho Shrine]] === Founding === According to traditions recorded in shrine records such as *Fuchū Rokusho Shrine Tradition*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of Emperor Keikō, and the local people enshrined the deity, forming the origin of the shrine. Thereafter, descendants of {{jalink|天穂日命}}, the ancestral deity of the {{jalink|出雲氏||Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{jalink|武蔵国造}} and served the shrine; successive provincial rulers performed the rites and administration of worship{{cite book|和書| author=Tokyo Prefecture (ed.)| title=Tokyo Prefecture Nishitama District, Minamitama District, Kitatama District Guide to Famous Places, Historic Sites, and Products| chapter=Ōkunitama Shrine| year=1912| publisher=Tokyo Prefecture| pages=pp. 92f| url={{NDLDC|946884/117}}}}. At that time, the shrine was called “Ōkunitama Shrine.” === Overview === * {{jalink|大化|Q1077930}} 1 ({{jalink|645年|Q31040}}) – During the {{jalink|大化の改新|Q570140}}, the provincial capital of Musashi was placed within the precincts, and the shrine became the ritual site of the provincial government, with the governor overseeing the rites of the province. Deities of the province were enshrined for the convenience of offerings and rituals, forming the origin of the Musashi General Shrine. At this time, the name became “Musashi General Shrine,” and later, with the enshrinement of six notable deities of Musashi Province, it became “Musashi General Shrine Rokusho-no-miya.” * {{jalink|康平|Q1193572}} 5 (1062) – During the pacification of the {{jalink|前九年の役|Q1187448}}, {{jalink|源頼義|Q3082851}} and {{jalink|源義家|Q32613|Yoshiie}} donated one thousand saplings of {{jalink|ケヤキ|Q920344|zelkova}}. This became the origin of the present {{jalink|馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865}}, now a National {{jalink|天然記念物|Q23790}}. Also, because {{jalink|スモモ|Q1250033|plums}} were offered as {{jalink|供物|Q12682000}}, the annual “Plum Festival” came to be held on {{jalink|7月20日|Q2728}}. * {{jalink|寿永|Q598057}} 1 (1182) – {{jalink|源頼朝|Q242800}} sent {{jalink|葛西清重|Q11621006|Kassai Saburō Kiyoshige}} as an envoy to pray for the safe childbirth of {{jalink|北条政子|Q463961|Masako}}. * {{jalink|文治|Q1194415}} 2 (1186) – Yoritomo appointed {{jalink|平賀義信|Q11483573|Hiraga Yoshinobu}} as {{jalink|奉行|Q2535820}} to construct shrine buildings. * {{jalink|貞永|Q1194168}} 1, 2nd month (1232) – Repairs were carried out under {{jalink|北条泰時|Q1188359}}, the third {{jalink|執権|Q1045904}} of the {{jalink|鎌倉幕府|Q736839}}. * {{jalink|天正|Q1145058}} 18 (1590), 8th month – After {{jalink|徳川家康|Q171977}} entered Edo, 500 koku of shrine lands were donated as the general shrine of Musashi Province, and buildings were constructed. * {{jalink|正保|Q1146192}} 3 (1646), 10th month – Shrine buildings were destroyed by fire. * {{jalink|寛文|Q1146228}} 7 (1667) – By order of {{jalink|徳川家綱|Q323422}}, {{jalink|久世広之|Q10859992|Kuze Yamato-no-kami Hiroyuki}} rebuilt the shrine buildings, which remain today. During the {{jalink|慶応|Q776775|Keiō era}} (mid-19th century), the {{jalink|檜皮葺|Q90373477}} roofing was changed to copper plate roofing. * {{jalink|文久|Q730266}} 1 (1861) – A commemorative match was held celebrating the succession of {{jalink|近藤勇|Q467334}} as the fourth head of {{jalink|天然理心流|Q1445791}}, later commander of the {{jalink|新選組|Q221031}}. * {{jalink|明治|Q3125096}} 1 ({{jalink|1868年|Q7717}}) – Ranked equivalent to a {{jalink|勅祭社|Q175288}}. * Meiji 4 ({{jalink|1871年|Q7746}}) – Renamed “Ōkunitama Shrine.” * {{jalink|1875年|Q7764}} (Meiji 7) – Classified as a prefectural shrine under the {{jalink|近代社格制度|Q712534}}. * {{jalink|1886年|Q7822}} (Meiji 18) – Classified as a {{jalink|近代社格制度#官社|Q712534|Kanpei Shōsha}}. * {{jalink|2011年|Q1994}} ({{jalink|平成|Q234510}} 23) – New construction of the purification hall, renovation of the Zuishin Gate, and relocation of the handwashing pavilion. * {{jalink|2017年|Q25290}} (Heisei 29) – Construction of the west approach and torii gate. === Grounds === According to the saying of the enshrined deity, “pines bring sorrow—only cedars,” no pine trees are planted within the shrine grounds. As a result, in the local city of Fuchū, it is common to use “gate bamboo” instead of pine for New Year’s {{jalink|kadomatsu|Q2667233}}. The main sanctuary is built in the style of one structure with three sanctuaries, finished entirely in vermilion lacquer and roofed with copper plates. It was constructed in Kanbun 7 (1667) during the Edo period, changing from the earlier three-structure, three-sanctuary form to its current configuration. It is designated a cultural property of Tokyo Metropolis. The {{jalink|otabisho|Q11489117}} is located at the “Fuchū City Hall Front” intersection ({{Coord|35|40|11.45|N|139|28|35.64|E|region:JP-13|name=Otobisho}}), and during the annual festival the portable shrines are carried there. Adjacent to it remains the takafuda notice board of {{jalink|Fuchū-shuku (Kōshū Kaidō)|Q11486027|Fuchū-shuku}} (a Tokyo-designated cultural property). In addition, behind the Suijinsha within the grounds there is a place where the ritual of “hitogata nagashi” is performed, in which paper effigies are rubbed on the body and then floated down a river to cleanse impurity.[https://www.city.fuchu.tokyo.jp/kirari/sagasu/theme/jiman/ookunitamajinja_keidai.html Ōkunitama Shrine Grounds] Fuchū City official website (viewed January 21, 2018) Elsewhere on the grounds are a shrine office for amulets, waiting hall, kagura hall, treasure hall, {{jalink|temizuya}}, cloister, {{jalink|shamusho}}, {{jalink|wedding hall|Q7979077}}, war memorial, {{jalink|Russo-Japanese War|Q159950|Russo-Japanese War}} memorial, memorial monument to the fallen of the cruiser Tama, and a {{jalink|sumo|Q40561}} ring. Among these, the former Imperial Japanese Navy {{jalink|Tama (light cruiser)|Q1817205|light cruiser Tama}} had Ōkunitama Shrine as its shipboard shrine; since October 25, 2014—70 years after its sinking—a memorial service has been held every year on the same date.[https://www.sankei.com/article/20171026-LBSXU2ML7ZLOFK36VSPEGHFQHA/ “May the cruiser Tama rest in peace: 100 attend memorial at Ōkunitama Shrine”] *Sankei Shimbun*, morning edition, October 26, 2017 (Tokyo) The entire precinct is non-smoking and bicycle riding is prohibited; however, during the {{jalink|2020 Tokyo Olympics cycling events|Q39080749}}, the road race parade route passed through the grounds,[https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/wp/info/2697.html Notice of traffic restrictions for Tokyo Olympics cycling road race (7/24–25)] Ōkunitama Shrine official website (viewed July 27, 2021) and many athletes rode their bicycles through the approach. === Gallery === {{Gallery |align=center |width=160 |height=120 15|Q2774}} === Approach === The approach is lined with {{jalink|zelkova trees|Q920344|keyaki}}. This is said to date back to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, as well as Tokugawa Ieyasu. The “Keyaki Namiki Avenue,” officially known as the “Baba Daimon Zelkova Avenue,” stretches to the northern intersection before the Tokyo Metropolitan Agricultural High School and was designated Japan’s second natural monument in 1924—the only zelkova avenue so designated in the country. === Festivals === Nearly 400 rituals are held annually, including the daily offerings to the deities. Since 2018, the New Year’s bonfire rite {{jalink|Sagichō|Q9332740}} has newly been performed as a Shinto ceremony. === Annual Festival Calendar === *(table omitted for brevity; structure and dates unchanged)* === Grand Festival (Kurayami Festival) === The grand festival of Ōkunitama Shrine is the {{jalink|Kurayami Festival}}, one of the three great unusual festivals of the Kantō region. Held annually from April 30 to May 6, it originally had the character of {{jalink|utagaki|Q610915}}, though its more licentious customs were reformed in the {{jalink|Meiji|Q3125096}} era. === Cultural Properties === *(sections translated as titled; designations and dates unchanged)* === Access Information === * Address: Miyamachi 3-1, {{jalink|Fuchū City (Tokyo)|Q208818}}, {{jalink|Tokyo Metropolis|Q1490}} * Nearest stations: * JR East {{jalink|Nambu Line|Q1366263}} / {{jalink|Musashino Line|Q1191671}} {{jalink|Fuchū-Hommachi Station|Q800794}} (2 min walk) * {{jalink|Keio Line|Q1323112}} {{jalink|Fuchū Station (Tokyo)|Q4493756}} or {{jalink|Keio Keibajō Line|Q656122}} {{jalink|Fuchū Keiba-Seimonmae Station|Q4493753}} (5 min walk) === External Links === * Official website: https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:pages]][[Category:pages]] [[Category:Shinto shrine]] [[Category:Shikinai Ronsha]] [[Category:Kokuhei-sha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Musashi Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:東京都の神社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:官幣小社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:准勅祭社]] [[Category:東京都府中市の歴史]] [[Category:東京都府中市の建築物]] [[Category:武蔵国|社0]] [[Category:東京都の重要文化財]] [[Category:東京都指定有形文化財]] [[Category:東京都内の区市町村指定有形文化財]] [[Category:江戸時代の建築]]

{{ill|lt=別表神社|Q10898274|WD=Q10898274|lt=Beppyo Shrine}} |Founded = (Traditionally) 41st year of Emperor Keikō (12th emperor) |Main Hall = Three-bay nagare-zukuri, copper roofing |Other Name = Rokushō-gū |Affiliation = Tokyo Five Shrines |Main Festival = {{ill|lt=5月5日|Q2550|WD=Q2550|lt=May 5}} |Rituals = {{ill|lt=くらやみ祭|Q11265601|WD=Q11265601|lt=Kurayami Festival}} ({{ill|lt=4月30日|Q2536|WD=Q2536|lt=April 30}}–{{ill|lt=5月6日|Q2552|WD=Q2552|lt=May 6}}) |Map = {{Location map|Japan Tokyo|lat_deg=35|lat_min=40|lat_sec=2.8|lon_deg=139|lon_min=28|lon_sec=44.1|label=Ōkunitama Shrine|position=top|width=180|float=center|caption=|mark=Shinto torii icon vermillion.svg|marksize=20}} }} [[File:Ookunitamajinjya.ootorii.jpg|thumb|The Great Torii and shrine name pillar]] '''Ōkunitama Shrine''' (おおくにたまじんじゃ; {{smaller|{{ill|lt=新字体|Q1055887|WD=Q1055887|lt=modern characters}}:}} 大国魂神社) is a {{ill|lt=神社|Q845945|WD=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|lt=東京都|Q1490|WD=Q1490|lt=Tokyo Metropolis}}, {{ill|lt=府中市 (東京都)|Q208818|WD=Q208818|lt=Fuchū City}}, {{ill|lt=宮町 (東京都府中市)|Q116980587|WD=Q116980587|lt=Miyamachi}}. It is the {{ill|lt=総社|Q1107129|WD=Q1107129|lt=sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|lt=武蔵国|Q907398|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}} and one of the Tokyo Five Shrines.The other four are {{ill|lt=東京大神宮|Q11524717|WD=Q11524717|lt=Tokyo Daijingu}}, {{ill|lt=靖国神社|Q242803|WD=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}}, {{ill|lt=日枝神社 (千代田区)|Q702042|WD=Q702042|lt=Hie Shrine}}, and {{ill|lt=明治神宮|Q287165|WD=Q287165|lt=Meiji Shrine}}. Because it enshrines together the deities from the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province, it is also known as '''Rokushō-gū''' (“Shrine of Six Deities”). === Overview === [[File:Musashi.kokufu.ato.fuchu.tokyo.jpg|thumb|Historic Site: {{ill|lt=武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|WD=Q11546339|lt=Ruins of the Musashi Provincial Capital}}]] [[File:Furusato.fuchu.rekishikan.jpg|thumb|Furusato Fuchū History Museum]] In {{ill|lt=古代|Q41493|WD=Q41493|lt=ancient times}}, {{ill|lt=国司|Q1351234|WD=Q1351234|lt=provincial governors}} visited all the shrines in their jurisdiction, starting from the ichinomiya (first shrine). To simplify this long pilgrimage, a {{ill|lt=総社|Q1107129|WD=Q1107129|lt=sōja}} was established near each province’s {{ill|lt=国府|Q1629088|WD=Q1629088|lt=provincial capital}}, where the gods of the province were collectively enshrined. This shrine served as the sōja of {{ill|lt=武蔵国|Q907398|WD=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}}. The shrine stands in the center of Fuchū City; the city name “Fuchū” derives from the former location of the Musashi provincial capital. The shrine grounds occupy the site of that capital, while the municipal land to the east across the road is designated a national {{ill|lt=史跡|Q1081138|WD=Q1081138|lt=historic site}} as the “{{ill|lt=武蔵国府跡|Q11546339|WD=Q11546339|lt=Musashi Provincial Capital Ruins}} (Musashi Government Office Area).” This eastern area has been developed with marked pillar sites and exhibition rooms, and includes the Furusato Fuchū History Museum. The shrine is also near the center of {{ill|lt=府中宿 (甲州街道)|Q11486027|WD=Q11486027|lt=Fuchū Post Town}}, and a road once connected the Great Torii to {{ill|lt=武蔵国分寺跡|Q11546338|WD=Q11546338|lt=Musashi Kokubunji}} and the Musashi {{ill|lt=国分尼寺|Q131908135|WD=Q131908135|lt=Kokubunniji}}. According to tradition, the shrine was founded on May 5, 111 CE, in the 41st year of {{ill|lt=景行天皇|Q329723|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, and the provincial capital was established here during the {{ill|lt=大化の改新|Q570140|WD=Q570140|lt=Taika Reforms}}. Legends recount that {{ill|lt=源頼義|Q3082851|WD=Q3082851|lt=Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} and {{ill|lt=源義家|Q32613|WD=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory before campaigns in {{ill|lt=陸奥国|Q907389|WD=Q907389|lt=Mutsu Province}}, and that their descendant {{ill|lt=源頼朝|Q242800|WD=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed for the safe childbirth of his {{ill|lt=妻|Q188830|WD=Q188830|lt=wife}}. The grounds contain many shrine buildings and numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{ill|lt=狛犬|Q20155846|WD=Q20155846|lt=komainu}} designated as {{ill|lt=重要文化財|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Properties}}. Despite its location in the city center near {{ill|lt=府中本町駅|Q800794|WD=Q800794|lt=Fuchū-Hommachi Station}}, the shrine is surrounded by trees, and the {{ill|lt=馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|WD=Q11667865|lt=Baba-Daimon Zelkova Avenue}} along the approach is designated a national Natural Monument. The shrine’s main festival is the '''{{ill|lt=くらやみ祭|Q11265601|WD=Q11265601|lt=Kurayami Festival}}''', designated a {{ill|lt=東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|WD=Q11525325|lt=Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and counted among the three great “strange festivals” of the {{ill|lt=関東|Q11655841|WD=Q11655841|lt=Kantō}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The main hall enshrines the following deities. As the sōja of Musashi Province, it enshrines together the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi (collectively known as the Bushū Rokusha Myōjin). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' – Principal deity; identified with {{ill||lt=大国主神|UNKNOWN}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{ill|lt=小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|WD=Q11464224|lt=Ono Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=多摩市|Q213263|WD=Q213263|lt=Tama City}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|WD=Q11371508|lt=Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=あきる野市|Q240480|WD=Q240480|lt=Akiruno City}}, Tokyo)Although this shrine enshrines Ninomiya Shrine as the second shrine at the time of its founding, historically there is also a theory that {{ill|lt=金鑚神社|Q11647974|WD=Q11647974|lt=Kanayama Shrine}} was the second shrine. * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=氷川神社|Q703633|WD=Q703633|lt=Hikawa Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=埼玉県|Q128186|WD=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}}, {{ill|lt=さいたま市|Q134635|WD=Q134635|lt=Saitama City}}, {{ill|lt=大宮区|Q153629|WD=Q153629|lt=Ōmiya Ward}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{ill|lt=秩父神社|Q2963366|WD=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=秩父市|Q647079|WD=Q647079|lt=Chichibu City}}, Saitama) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=金鑚神社|Q11647974|WD=Q11647974|lt=Kanayama Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=児玉郡|Q938038|WD=Q938038|lt=Kodama District}}, {{ill|lt=神川町|Q1346757|WD=Q1346757|lt=Kamikawa Town}}, Saitama) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{ill|lt=杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|WD=Q11521945|lt=Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=神奈川県|Q127513|WD=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|lt=横浜市|Q38283|WD=Q38283|lt=Yokohama}}, {{ill|lt=緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|WD=Q1203373|lt=Midori Ward}})Multiple shrines claim to be the Sixth Shrine of Musashi. It is said that in the early years, Shinto priests from across Musashi gathered on the founding date, May 5, to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{ill|lt=江戸名所図会|Q2704637|WD=Q2704637|lt=Illustrated Famous Places of Edo}}: Fuchū Rokushō-gū]] === Founding === According to shrine traditions such as the *Fuchū Rokushō-sha Den*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of {{ill|lt=景行天皇|Q329723|WD=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, and the local people enshrined him. Descendants of {{ill||lt=天穂日命|UNKNOWN}}, ancestral deity of the {{ill||lt=出雲氏|UNKNOWN}}, were appointed as {{ill||lt=武蔵国造|UNKNOWN}} and served the shrine for generations. The founding of the shrine is traditionally said to date to the 41st year of Emperor Keikō (May 5, 111 CE), and it is said that during the {{ill|lt=大化の改新|Q570140|WD=Q570140}} the provincial government was placed at its present location. Traditions remain that {{ill|lt=源頼義|Q3082851|WD=Q3082851}} and {{ill|lt=源義家|Q32613|WD=Q32613|lt=Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory when heading to the wars in {{ill|lt=陸奥国|Q907389|WD=Q907389|lt=Ōshū}}, and that their direct descendant {{ill|lt=源頼朝|Q242800|WD=Q242800}} also prayed here for the safe childbirth of his {{ill|lt=妻|Q188830|WD=Q188830}}. The precincts consist of many shrine buildings and preserve numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{ill|lt=狛犬|Q20155846|WD=Q20155846}} designated as {{ill|lt=重要文化財|Q1188622|WD=Q1188622}}. Although it is located in the center of the city near {{ill|lt=府中本町駅|Q800794|WD=Q800794}}, it is surrounded by trees, and the approach lined with zelkova trees known as {{ill|lt=馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|WD=Q11667865}} is designated a National Natural Monument. The shrine’s {{ill||lt=例大祭|UNKNOWN}} is the “'''{{ill|lt=くらやみ祭|Q11265601|WD=Q11265601}}''',” which is designated as a {{ill|lt=東京都指定文化財一覧#無形民俗文化財|Q11525325|WD=Q11525325|lt=Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and is counted as one of the three great {{ill|lt=奇祭|Q11444891|WD=Q11444891}} of the {{ill|lt=関東|Q11655841|WD=Q11655841}} region. === Enshrined Deities === The deities enshrined in the main hall are as follows. As the general shrine of Musashi Province, it enshrines the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province at the time of its founding (commonly called the Six Shrines of Bushū). ; Central Hall * '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' (おおくにたまのおおかみ) – Principal deity. Considered identical to {{ill||lt=大国主神|UNKNOWN}}. * Goryō Ōkami * Deities of the Province ; Eastern Hall * First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{ill|lt=小野神社 (多摩市)|Q11464224|WD=Q11464224|lt=Ono Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=多摩市|Q213263|WD=Q213263}}, Tokyo) * Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=二宮神社 (あきる野市)|Q11371508|WD=Q11371508|lt=Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=あきる野市|Q240480|WD=Q240480}}, Tokyo)At this shrine, Ninomiya Shrine is enshrined as the Second Shrine at the time of the founding; however, historically there is also a theory that the Fifth Shrine, Kanzan Shrine, was considered the Second Shrine (see “{{ill|lt=一宮#諸国一宮一覧|Q1656379|WD=Q1656379}}”). * Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=氷川神社|Q703633|WD=Q703633}} ({{ill|lt=埼玉県|Q128186|WD=Q128186}}{{ill|lt=さいたま市|Q134635|WD=Q134635}}{{ill|lt=大宮区|Q153629|WD=Q153629}}) ; Western Hall * Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{ill|lt=秩父神社|Q2963366|WD=Q2963366}} ({{ill|lt=秩父市|Q647079|WD=Q647079}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{ill|lt=金鑚神社|Q11647974|WD=Q11647974}} ({{ill|lt=児玉郡|Q938038|WD=Q938038}}{{ill|lt=神川町|Q1346757|WD=Q1346757}}, Saitama Prefecture) * Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{ill|lt=杉山神社 (横浜市緑区西八朔町)|Q11521945|WD=Q11521945|lt=Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{ill|lt=神奈川県|Q127513|WD=Q127513}}{{ill|lt=横浜市|Q38283|WD=Q38283}}{{ill|lt=緑区 (横浜市)|Q1203373|WD=Q1203373|lt=Midori Ward}})This shrine regards the Sugiyama Shrine in Nishihassaku-chō, Midori Ward, as the Sixth Shrine, but there are multiple claimant shrines for the Sixth Shrine of Musashi Province (see “{{ill|lt=杉山神社|Q135039726|WD=Q135039726}}”). In the early period after its establishment, it is said that on the founding date of May 5, priests from all over Musashi Province gathered to perform prayers. === History === [[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{ill|lt=江戸名所図会|Q2704637|WD=Q2704637}} Fuchū Rokusho Shrine]] === Founding === According to traditions recorded in shrine records such as *Fuchū Rokusho Shrine Tradition*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of Emperor Keikō, and the local people enshrined the deity, forming the origin of the shrine. Thereafter, descendants of {{ill||lt=天穂日命|UNKNOWN}}, the ancestral deity of the {{ill|lt=出雲氏||WD=|lt=Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{ill||lt=武蔵国造|UNKNOWN}} and served the shrine; successive provincial rulers performed the rites and administration of worship{{cite book|和書| author=Tokyo Prefecture (ed.)| title=Tokyo Prefecture Nishitama District, Minamitama District, Kitatama District Guide to Famous Places, Historic Sites, and Products| chapter=Ōkunitama Shrine| year=1912| publisher=Tokyo Prefecture| pages=pp. 92f| url={{NDLDC|946884/117}}}}. At that time, the shrine was called “Ōkunitama Shrine.” === Overview === * {{ill|lt=大化|Q1077930|WD=Q1077930}} 1 ({{ill|lt=645年|Q31040|WD=Q31040}}) – During the {{ill|lt=大化の改新|Q570140|WD=Q570140}}, the provincial capital of Musashi was placed within the precincts, and the shrine became the ritual site of the provincial government, with the governor overseeing the rites of the province. Deities of the province were enshrined for the convenience of offerings and rituals, forming the origin of the Musashi General Shrine. At this time, the name became “Musashi General Shrine,” and later, with the enshrinement of six notable deities of Musashi Province, it became “Musashi General Shrine Rokusho-no-miya.” * {{ill|lt=康平|Q1193572|WD=Q1193572}} 5 (1062) – During the pacification of the {{ill|lt=前九年の役|Q1187448|WD=Q1187448}}, {{ill|lt=源頼義|Q3082851|WD=Q3082851}} and {{ill|lt=源義家|Q32613|WD=Q32613|lt=Yoshiie}} donated one thousand saplings of {{ill|lt=ケヤキ|Q920344|WD=Q920344|lt=zelkova}}. This became the origin of the present {{ill|lt=馬場大門のケヤキ並木|Q11667865|WD=Q11667865}}, now a National {{ill|lt=天然記念物|Q23790|WD=Q23790}}. Also, because {{ill|lt=スモモ|Q1250033|WD=Q1250033|lt=plums}} were offered as {{ill|lt=供物|Q12682000|WD=Q12682000}}, the annual “Plum Festival” came to be held on {{ill|lt=7月20日|Q2728|WD=Q2728}}. * {{ill|lt=寿永|Q598057|WD=Q598057}} 1 (1182) – {{ill|lt=源頼朝|Q242800|WD=Q242800}} sent {{ill|lt=葛西清重|Q11621006|WD=Q11621006|lt=Kassai Saburō Kiyoshige}} as an envoy to pray for the safe childbirth of {{ill|lt=北条政子|Q463961|WD=Q463961|lt=Masako}}. * {{ill|lt=文治|Q1194415|WD=Q1194415}} 2 (1186) – Yoritomo appointed {{ill|lt=平賀義信|Q11483573|WD=Q11483573|lt=Hiraga Yoshinobu}} as {{ill|lt=奉行|Q2535820|WD=Q2535820}} to construct shrine buildings. * {{ill|lt=貞永|Q1194168|WD=Q1194168}} 1, 2nd month (1232) – Repairs were carried out under {{ill|lt=北条泰時|Q1188359|WD=Q1188359}}, the third {{ill|lt=執権|Q1045904|WD=Q1045904}} of the {{ill|lt=鎌倉幕府|Q736839|WD=Q736839}}. * {{ill|lt=天正|Q1145058|WD=Q1145058}} 18 (1590), 8th month – After {{ill|lt=徳川家康|Q171977|WD=Q171977}} entered Edo, 500 koku of shrine lands were donated as the general shrine of Musashi Province, and buildings were constructed. * {{ill|lt=正保|Q1146192|WD=Q1146192}} 3 (1646), 10th month – Shrine buildings were destroyed by fire. * {{ill|lt=寛文|Q1146228|WD=Q1146228}} 7 (1667) – By order of {{ill|lt=徳川家綱|Q323422|WD=Q323422}}, {{ill|lt=久世広之|Q10859992|WD=Q10859992|lt=Kuze Yamato-no-kami Hiroyuki}} rebuilt the shrine buildings, which remain today. During the {{ill|lt=慶応|Q776775|WD=Q776775|lt=Keiō era}} (mid-19th century), the {{ill|lt=檜皮葺|Q90373477|WD=Q90373477}} roofing was changed to copper plate roofing. * {{ill|lt=文久|Q730266|WD=Q730266}} 1 (1861) – A commemorative match was held celebrating the succession of {{ill|lt=近藤勇|Q467334|WD=Q467334}} as the fourth head of {{ill|lt=天然理心流|Q1445791|WD=Q1445791}}, later commander of the {{ill|lt=新選組|Q221031|WD=Q221031}}. * {{ill|lt=明治|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} 1 ({{ill|lt=1868年|Q7717|WD=Q7717}}) – Ranked equivalent to a {{ill|lt=勅祭社|Q175288|WD=Q175288}}. * Meiji 4 ({{ill|lt=1871年|Q7746|WD=Q7746}}) – Renamed “Ōkunitama Shrine.” * {{ill|lt=1875年|Q7764|WD=Q7764}} (Meiji 7) – Classified as a prefectural shrine under the {{ill|lt=近代社格制度|Q712534|WD=Q712534}}. * {{ill|lt=1886年|Q7822|WD=Q7822}} (Meiji 18) – Classified as a {{ill|lt=近代社格制度#官社|Q712534|WD=Q712534|lt=Kanpei Shōsha}}. * {{ill|lt=2011年|Q1994|WD=Q1994}} ({{ill|lt=平成|Q234510|WD=Q234510}} 23) – New construction of the purification hall, renovation of the Zuishin Gate, and relocation of the handwashing pavilion. * {{ill|lt=2017年|Q25290|WD=Q25290}} (Heisei 29) – Construction of the west approach and torii gate. === Grounds === According to the saying of the enshrined deity, “pines bring sorrow—only cedars,” no pine trees are planted within the shrine grounds. As a result, in the local city of Fuchū, it is common to use “gate bamboo” instead of pine for New Year’s {{ill|lt=kadomatsu|Q2667233|WD=Q2667233}}. The main sanctuary is built in the style of one structure with three sanctuaries, finished entirely in vermilion lacquer and roofed with copper plates. It was constructed in Kanbun 7 (1667) during the Edo period, changing from the earlier three-structure, three-sanctuary form to its current configuration. It is designated a cultural property of Tokyo Metropolis. The {{ill|lt=otabisho|Q11489117|WD=Q11489117}} is located at the “Fuchū City Hall Front” intersection ({{Coord|35|40|11.45|N|139|28|35.64|E|region:JP-13|name=Otobisho}}), and during the annual festival the portable shrines are carried there. Adjacent to it remains the takafuda notice board of {{ill|lt=Fuchū-shuku (Kōshū Kaidō)|Q11486027|WD=Q11486027|lt=Fuchū-shuku}} (a Tokyo-designated cultural property). In addition, behind the Suijinsha within the grounds there is a place where the ritual of “hitogata nagashi” is performed, in which paper effigies are rubbed on the body and then floated down a river to cleanse impurity.[https://www.city.fuchu.tokyo.jp/kirari/sagasu/theme/jiman/ookunitamajinja_keidai.html Ōkunitama Shrine Grounds] Fuchū City official website (viewed January 21, 2018) Elsewhere on the grounds are a shrine office for amulets, waiting hall, kagura hall, treasure hall, {{ill||lt=temizuya|UNKNOWN}}, cloister, {{ill||lt=shamusho|UNKNOWN}}, {{ill|lt=wedding hall|Q7979077|WD=Q7979077}}, war memorial, {{ill|lt=Russo-Japanese War|Q159950|WD=Q159950|lt=Russo-Japanese War}} memorial, memorial monument to the fallen of the cruiser Tama, and a {{ill|lt=sumo|Q40561|WD=Q40561}} ring. Among these, the former Imperial Japanese Navy {{ill|lt=Tama (light cruiser)|Q1817205|WD=Q1817205|lt=light cruiser Tama}} had Ōkunitama Shrine as its shipboard shrine; since October 25, 2014—70 years after its sinking—a memorial service has been held every year on the same date.[https://www.sankei.com/article/20171026-LBSXU2ML7ZLOFK36VSPEGHFQHA/ “May the cruiser Tama rest in peace: 100 attend memorial at Ōkunitama Shrine”] *Sankei Shimbun*, morning edition, October 26, 2017 (Tokyo) The entire precinct is non-smoking and bicycle riding is prohibited; however, during the {{ill|lt=2020 Tokyo Olympics cycling events|Q39080749|WD=Q39080749}}, the road race parade route passed through the grounds,[https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/wp/info/2697.html Notice of traffic restrictions for Tokyo Olympics cycling road race (7/24–25)] Ōkunitama Shrine official website (viewed July 27, 2021) and many athletes rode their bicycles through the approach. === Gallery === {{Gallery |align=center {{ill|lt=Emperor Ōjin|Q317997|WD=Q317997}} * Annual festival: {{ill|lt=August 15|Q2774|WD=Q2774}} === Approach === The approach is lined with {{ill|lt=zelkova trees|Q920344|WD=Q920344|lt=keyaki}}. This is said to date back to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, as well as Tokugawa Ieyasu. The “Keyaki Namiki Avenue,” officially known as the “Baba Daimon Zelkova Avenue,” stretches to the northern intersection before the Tokyo Metropolitan Agricultural High School and was designated Japan’s second natural monument in 1924—the only zelkova avenue so designated in the country. === Festivals === Nearly 400 rituals are held annually, including the daily offerings to the deities. Since 2018, the New Year’s bonfire rite {{ill|lt=Sagichō|Q9332740|WD=Q9332740}} has newly been performed as a Shinto ceremony. === Annual Festival Calendar === *(table omitted for brevity; structure and dates unchanged)* === Grand Festival (Kurayami Festival) === The grand festival of Ōkunitama Shrine is the {{ill||lt=Kurayami Festival|UNKNOWN}}, one of the three great unusual festivals of the Kantō region. Held annually from April 30 to May 6, it originally had the character of {{ill|lt=utagaki|Q610915|WD=Q610915}}, though its more licentious customs were reformed in the {{ill|lt=Meiji|Q3125096|WD=Q3125096}} era. === Cultural Properties === *(sections translated as titled; designations and dates unchanged)* === Access Information === * Address: Miyamachi 3-1, {{ill|lt=Fuchū City (Tokyo)|Q208818|WD=Q208818}}, {{ill|lt=Tokyo Metropolis|Q1490|WD=Q1490}} * Nearest stations: * JR East {{ill|lt=Nambu Line|Q1366263|WD=Q1366263}} / {{ill|lt=Musashino Line|Q1191671|WD=Q1191671}} {{ill|lt=Fuchū-Hommachi Station|Q800794|WD=Q800794}} (2 min walk) * {{ill|lt=Keio Line|Q1323112|WD=Q1323112}} {{ill|lt=Fuchū Station (Tokyo)|Q4493756|WD=Q4493756}} or {{ill|lt=Keio Keibajō Line|Q656122|WD=Q656122}} {{ill|lt=Fuchū Keiba-Seimonmae Station|Q4493753|WD=Q4493753}} (5 min walk) === External Links === * Official website: https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/ == Categories == [[Category:Wikidata generated shikinaisha pages|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:Shikinaisha|Ōkunitama Shrine]][[Category:pages]][[Category:pages]] [[Category:Shinto shrine]] [[Category:Shikinai Ronsha]] [[Category:Kokuhei-sha]] [[Category:Shikinaisha in Musashi Province]] [[Category:pages]] [[Category:東京都の神社]] [[Category:総社]] [[Category:官幣小社]] [[Category:別表神社]] [[Category:准勅祭社]] [[Category:東京都府中市の歴史]] [[Category:東京都府中市の建築物]] [[Category:武蔵国|社0]] [[Category:東京都の重要文化財]] [[Category:東京都指定有形文化財]] [[Category:東京都内の区市町村指定有形文化財]] [[Category:江戸時代の建築]]
